strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: fine-tuning diffusion models for non-differentiable, scientifically relevant rewards in biomolecular design (proteins, DNA, small molecules), which is underexplored relative to differentiable reward fine-tuning in vision.

Provides a clean theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) formally connecting PPO-style fine-tuning objectives to reverse KL minimization between trajectory distributions, giving a principled explanation for why on-policy RL methods may be unstable/mode-seeking, and contrasting this with the proposed forward-KL/off-policy distillation objective.

The proposed VIDD algorithm is a reasonably natural and practical instantiation of value-weighted MLE / soft-optimal policy distillation for diffusion models, with a clearly described roll-in/roll-out/distillation procedure and a computationally cheap value approximation (single denoiser forward pass).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three distinct biomolecular modalities (protein sequences via EvoDiff, regulatory DNA via masked diffusion, small molecules via GDSS) and several reward types (structure-based, affinity-based, docking-based), compared against multiple relevant baselines (SFT, DDPO, DDPP, DRAKES, Best-of-N).

Good supplementary analysis: ablations on the lazy update interval K, the roll-in mixture coefficient β, reward–diversity trade-off scatter/training curves, combination with inference-time techniques (Best-of-N), and detailed molecule-quality metrics (validity, novelty, FCD, NSPDK, stability), which strengthen the empirical credibility of the results.
Reasonably thorough documentation of hyperparameters, task/reward definitions, and licensing in the appendix, aiding reproducibility despite some gaps.
weaknesses: The core soft-value approximation (replacing the expectation in Eq. 3 with a single posterior-mean plug-in r(x̂0(xt))) is a strong heuristic, particularly inaccurate at high noise levels (large t); no ablation or empirical validation is provided comparing this approximation against Monte Carlo or learned value estimates, despite it being central to the method's theoretical justification.

Reward–diversity trade-off is only partially reconciled: for several tasks (e.g., PD-L1, IFNAR2, SS-match) diversity drops substantially relative to the pretrained model and is comparable to or only marginally better than DDPO, which is in some tension with the paper's central claim that forward-KL/off-policy training mitigates the mode collapse associated with reverse-KL/on-policy PPO methods.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are reported as 50% quantiles with wide confidence intervals in multiple cells, but no significance testing or discussion of overlap between VIDD and the strongest baseline (often DDPO) is provided, making some of the reported "wins" hard to assess conclusively.

Reproducibility is undermined by the missing/broken code release link ("The source code is released at ."), and it is unclear whether baseline methods (DDPO, DDPP, SFT) were given comparable hyperparameter tuning budgets to VIDD, raising concerns about fairness of comparisons.

The method introduces several additional hyperparameters (α, K, β schedule, roll-in mixture) whose sensitivity is only explored for K on one task (DNA); the practical burden of tuning these across new domains/rewards is not well characterized.

The theoretical results (Theorem 1, off-policy justification) are somewhat disconnected from the final practical algorithm, which relies on approximations (plug-in value estimates, lazy target updates) whose convergence properties are not analyzed, leaving a gap between the clean theory and the heuristic practice.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (DDPO) are inconsistent in magnitude across tasks — large in some (e.g., IFNAR2 reward, DNA Pred-Activity/ATAC-Acc, molecule NLL) but modest in others (e.g., protein β-sheet%, PD-L1 ipTM), suggesting the method's advantage may be task-dependent rather than uniformly strong.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: fine-tuning diffusion models for non-differentiable, scientifically-motivated rewards in protein/DNA/molecule design.
Provides a clean theoretical connection (Theorem 1) showing PPO-style objectives correspond to reverse KL minimization, motivating the switch to a forward-KL/value-weighted objective.
Evaluates across three distinct biomolecular domains (protein, DNA, small molecule) with multiple reward types, which is a reasonably broad empirical scope.
Includes several ablations (lazy update interval K, roll-in mixture coefficient beta) and additional appendix results combining the method with inference-time techniques.

Algorithm description (roll-in/roll-out/distillation) is implemented with practical approximations (posterior-mean value estimate) that avoid training extra value networks, which is a sensible engineering choice.
weaknesses: The paper's central claim—that forward-KL/off-policy distillation avoids the mode-seeking collapse of PPO—is directly contradicted by its own results: VIDD shows a large diversity drop relative to the pretrained model in binder design (e.g., PD-L1 diversity falls from 0.90 to 0.55, IFNAR2 from 0.90 to 0.52), comparable to or worse than DDPO in several cases, undermining the stated motivation.

Core algorithmic idea is essentially advantage-/value-weighted regression (Peng et al. 2019, Peters et al. 2010) applied to the diffusion denoising process; the technical novelty beyond adapting this known offline-RL technique to diffusion fine-tuning is limited.

Reported results lack rigorous statistical validation—no indication of multiple random seeds, no significance testing, and many comparisons (e.g., identical 0.52 diversity for DDPO and VIDD on SS-match) look suspicious or possibly erroneous.

Baseline comparison is narrow: only DDPO, DDPP, and SFT are compared as fine-tuning baselines; several directly relevant recent works cited in related work (e.g., Zekri & Boullé 2025, Gupta et al. 2025) are not empirically compared.

Reward functions used (ipTM, Enformer activity, docking scores) are themselves proxy/learned models susceptible to reward hacking; the paper claims robustness to over-optimization (via ATAC-Acc) but this is only checked for one task (DNA) and not systematically analyzed.

Hyperparameters (alpha, K, batch size, learning rate) differ substantially across tasks with no discussion of sensitivity or principled selection, raising concerns about generalizability and fair tuning effort relative to baselines.

The improvement in NLL for molecule generation (741 vs. 971) is presented as a positive but could equally indicate distributional collapse toward low-likelihood/overfit samples optimizing the docking score; this is not carefully disambiguated from desirable 'naturalness'.
Writing contains some unclear/grammatically broken passages (e.g., end of Section 3.1), and the abstract leaves the code repository link blank, limiting reproducibility verification at review time.

Figures 5 and 6 used to support the reward-diversity trade-off argument are only qualitative scatter/training-curve plots without quantitative summary statistics, weakening the strength of the empirical claim they are meant to support.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated theoretical framing: the paper formally shows (Theorem 1, with proof in the appendix) that PPO-style fine-tuning implicitly minimizes a reverse KL divergence to the soft-optimal trajectory distribution, and contrasts this with VIDD's forward-KL/value-weighted MLE objective, giving a principled explanation for the claimed stability gains.

Broad and fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three distinct biomolecular design modalities (protein sequence/binder design, regulatory DNA, small molecules) with multiple reward functions and baselines (SFT, DDPO, DDPP, DRAKES, Best-of-N), which is more extensive than most comparable single-domain papers.

Reasonably thorough ablations and auxiliary analyses: lazy update interval K, roll-in mixture coefficient β, reward-diversity tradeoff curves/scatter plots, combination with inference-time Best-of-N, and extensive molecule-quality metrics (validity, novelty, FCD, NSPDK MMD, stability).

The practical approximation of the soft value function via a single forward pass (r(x̂0)) is computationally efficient and clearly explained, and the overall algorithm (roll-in/roll-out/distillation) is described in sufficient algorithmic detail (Algorithm 1) to be implementable.

Results generally show consistent improvements over RL-style baselines (DDPO) and other fine-tuning baselines across most primary reward metrics, including outperforming a direct-backprop method (DRAKES) on the (differentiable) DNA task.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic idea is closely related to existing value-weighted/advantage-weighted regression and offline RL methods (e.g., Peters et al. 2010; Peng et al. 2019 AWR) and to prior reward-weighted fine-tuning/distillation approaches (DDPP); the novelty lies mainly in adapting this to the diffusion denoising process rather than in a fundamentally new algorithmic idea, which somewhat limits the significance of the contribution.

The claim that VIDD approximates a forward KL objective is treated less rigorously than the reverse-KL equivalence for PPO (Theorem 1); no analogous formal theorem/proof is given for the forward-KL claim, leaving an asymmetry in the theoretical rigor of the two main claims.

The soft value function approximation v̂(x_t) ≈ r(x̂0(x_t)) replaces a conditional expectation with a point estimate (posterior mean plug-in), which could introduce non-trivial bias, especially at early/noisy timesteps; this approximation is not theoretically analyzed and its effect on fidelity to the true soft-optimal policy is not quantified.

Diversity sometimes drops substantially for VIDD relative to baselines (e.g., diversity ~0.52 for PD-L1/SS-match vs. ~0.90 for pretrained/DDPP), and some secondary metrics are notably worse than baselines (e.g., 3-mer correlation 0.162 for VIDD vs. 0.879 for DDPP on DNA), which is not fully reconciled despite the reward-diversity tradeoff discussion.

No explicit comparison of computational cost/sample efficiency (e.g., number of reward-function evaluations, wall-clock time, number of gradient updates) between VIDD and baselines, despite sample efficiency being one of the paper's central claimed advantages.

Reproducibility is limited: the source code link is a placeholder (not actually provided), and several experimental/implementation details (e.g., exact network architectures for fine-tuned models, full training procedures per task) are relegated to brief appendix tables without enough specificity to fully reproduce results.

The baseline selection, while reasonable, omits some other recent related methods explicitly cited in the related work (e.g., SVDD, Zekri & Boullé 2025, Venkatraman et al. 2024) from the main quantitative comparison tables, despite being discussed as relevant alternatives.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: fine-tuning diffusion models with non-differentiable rewards common in biomolecular design (structure matching, docking scores, binding affinity).

Provides a clean theoretical framing connecting policy-gradient/PPO-style fine-tuning to reverse KL minimization (Theorem 1) and contrasts it with their forward-KL, off-policy distillation objective, giving intuitive justification for improved stability.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three distinct biomolecular modalities (protein sequences, regulatory DNA, small molecules) with multiple reward functions, and comparisons against several relevant baselines (SFT, DDPO, DDPP, DRAKES, Best-of-N).

Thorough ablation studies in the appendix covering lazy update interval, regularization coefficient, roll-in mixture ratio, value function approximation choices (posterior mean vs Monte Carlo vs learned critic), and robustness to noisy rewards.

Practical algorithmic design choices (lazy roll-out updates, mixture roll-in) are well-motivated and empirically validated, and the paper is transparent about limitations (reward misspecification, over-optimization, tuning needs).
Includes reward-diversity trade-off analysis and visualizations (structures, docking poses) that add qualitative support to quantitative claims.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic idea closely mirrors existing value-weighted / advantage-weighted regression (AWR) style off-policy RL methods (e.g., Peng et al. 2019, Peters et al. 2010) adapted to the diffusion denoising setting; the novelty is primarily in the application and specific value approximation rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic principle.

The soft value function is approximated by a single posterior-mean point estimate (r(x̂0)) rather than the true conditional expectation in Eq. 3; this crude approximation, especially at high noise levels (large t), is not rigorously justified theoretically, only empirically motivated by prior inference-time methods.

Some results raise reward over-optimization/hacking concerns that are insufficiently addressed: e.g., on the DNA task VIDD achieves much lower 3-mer correlation (0.162) than DDPP (0.879) or DRAKES (0.887) despite comparable or better reward and ATAC-Acc scores, suggesting the generated sequences may deviate substantially from natural sequence statistics.

Many reported metrics have large confidence intervals/standard errors (e.g., diversity, radius, pLDDT in protein tasks), and the number of random seeds/runs used is not clearly stated, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported improvements over baselines.

Despite claiming improved 'sample efficiency' relative to on-policy RL methods, the paper provides no direct wall-clock time, gradient-step, or reward-query-count comparison against baselines to substantiate this efficiency claim.

Theorem 1's connection between the on-policy PPO objective and reverse KL is derived under a specific idealized setting and its practical relevance to the actual empirical instability observed in DDPO/DDPP is asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated (e.g., no direct empirical measurement of forward vs reverse KL divergence during training).

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: fine-tuning diffusion models with non-differentiable, scientifically-motivated reward functions in protein, DNA, and small-molecule design.

Provides a clean theoretical connection (Theorem 1) showing that PPO-style fine-tuning of diffusion models implicitly minimizes a reverse KL divergence to the soft-optimal policy, motivating the switch to a forward-KL/value-weighted distillation objective.

Broad empirical coverage across three biomolecular modalities (protein sequence/binder design, regulatory DNA, small molecule docking) with several relevant baselines (DDPO, DDPP, SFT, Best-of-N, DRAKES).

Extensive appendix ablations (lazy update interval K, regularization coefficient α, roll-in mixture β, soft-value estimator choice, reward-noise robustness) that attempt to characterize the method's sensitivity and design choices.
Reasonable presentation with structural visualizations and docking renderings that make the qualitative gains more tangible.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim—that forward-KL-based VIDD avoids the mode-seeking/mode-collapse behavior attributed to PPO-style reverse-KL methods like DDPO—is not supported by the paper's own diversity numbers: in Table 1 (SS-match) VIDD and DDPO report nearly identical diversity (0.52 vs 0.52), and in Table 2 VIDD's diversity (0.55/0.52) is comparable to or only marginally better than DDPO's (0.53/0.72) and far below the pretrained model's (~0.90–0.91), directly undercutting the paper's key theoretical selling point.

Appendix ablations (e.g., Table 16–18) show large, non-monotonic performance swings as a function of the lazy-update interval K and regularization coefficient α (e.g., reward fluctuating from 0.19 to 0.91 for PD-L1 depending on K), which contradicts the claimed training-stability advantage over PPO-based methods and suggests the method itself is heavily hyperparameter-sensitive and requires per-task tuning.

The core algorithmic idea—value/reward-weighted maximum likelihood distillation with periodic (lazy) target updates—closely mirrors existing off-policy RL techniques (AWR/RWR, Peng et al. 2019; policy distillation, Czarnecki et al. 2019) that are explicitly cited as inspiration; the novelty is largely in combining these known ideas and applying a simple posterior-mean value approximation to a new application domain, rather than a substantively new algorithmic or theoretical contribution.

The soft-value approximation used throughout (single posterior-mean/argmax decoding, vt(xt) ≈ r(x̂0(xt))) is a fairly crude, high-variance/high-bias surrogate for the true expectation in Eq. (3); the paper's own Monte Carlo ablation (Appendix F.2) shows this approximation is not robustly better and offers limited theoretical justification for why it should work well across highly non-convex, non-differentiable rewards.

Robustness analysis (Appendix G) shows substantial performance degradation under even modest (10%) reward noise (e.g., PD-L1 reward drops from 0.91 to 0.47, IFNAR2 from 0.51 to 0.20), which is concerning given that the paper's stated motivation is exactly the noisy, non-differentiable, simulation-based rewards common in biomolecular design; this limitation is acknowledged but not addressed.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat uneven: DRAKES (a strong gradient-based baseline) is only evaluated on the one differentiable-reward task (DNA), and no attempt is made to construct an analogous differentiable-surrogate baseline for the protein/molecule tasks, making the comparisons across domains less uniform; also Best-of-N is dismissed as impractical rather than rigorously compared on an equal compute budget.

Several reported numbers raise reproducibility/robustness questions without further scrutiny (e.g., identical diversity values to two decimal places between VIDD and DDPO in Table 1; wide confidence intervals in several cells, e.g., DDPO ATAC-Acc 0.086 ± 0.280), and it is unclear how many random seeds/runs underlie the reported standard errors.

No wall-clock or compute-cost comparison is provided between VIDD and the RL baselines (DDPO, DDPP), despite sample-efficiency and training-stability being central claimed advantages of the proposed off-policy approach.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem—fine-tuning diffusion models under non-differentiable reward functions—with clear motivation grounded in real biomolecular design settings (DSSP, AlphaFold-based rewards, docking scores).

Provides a clean theoretical framing that connects PPO-style fine-tuning to reverse KL minimization (Theorem 1) and contrasts it with the proposed forward-KL/value-weighted MLE objective, giving the method interpretable grounding in the RL literature (RWR/AWR, policy distillation).

Broad and fairly rigorous empirical evaluation spanning three very different modalities (protein sequence/structure, regulatory DNA, small molecules) and multiple reward types, with consistent gains over DDPO, DDPP, standard fine-tuning, and even the differentiable-reward baseline DRAKES on one metric.

Extensive ablations in the appendix (lazy-update interval K, regularization coefficient α, roll-in mixture β, choice of value estimator, reward noise robustness, combination with inference-time Best-of-N) that give good insight into the algorithm's behavior and practical sensitivities.
Explicit analysis of the reward–diversity trade-off via training curves and scatter plots, addressing a natural concern about mode collapse that the method is designed to avoid.
Reasonably thorough and transparent reporting of limitations (imperfect/noisy reward functions, hyperparameter sensitivity, scalability of value networks) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: the method is essentially value-weighted MLE / advantage-weighted regression (Peng et al., 2019) applied to the diffusion denoising process, combined with a posterior-mean value approximation that has already been used in inference-time guidance work (e.g., SVDD/Li et al., 2024). The main new ingredients (off-policy roll-in mixture, lazy target updates) are reasonable engineering choices but lack deep theoretical novelty or convergence guarantees.

The soft value function is approximated by a single point estimate r(x̂0) rather than a proper expectation; the paper's own Monte Carlo ablation shows this crude approximation outperforming MC averaging, which is counterintuitive and not well explained theoretically—raising concerns about whether the claimed 'soft-optimal policy' distillation is actually being approximated faithfully in practice.

Results are mixed in places that undercut some claims: e.g., VIDD's 3-mer correlation on DNA design is substantially lower than baselines (0.162 vs 0.879 for DDPP), and diversity in the SS-match task is identical to DDPO (0.52), suggesting the reward-diversity benefits are not uniformly realized across tasks/metrics.

Performance appears quite sensitive to hyperparameters such as the lazy-update interval K and the roll-in mixture coefficient β (e.g., Table 16–18 show large swings in reward and diversity across K values), with no principled or adaptive scheme proposed—this is acknowledged as future work but reduces practical robustness of the method as presented.

No formal convergence or error-bound analysis is provided for the iterative distillation procedure with lazy, periodically-updated targets; the justification is only via informal analogy to the Policy Improvement Theorem.
Baseline tuning details (e.g., for DDPO, DDPP) are not fully transparent, making it harder to assess whether reported gaps reflect genuine algorithmic advantages versus differences in tuning effort.

No mention of code/data release for reproducibility, which is a concern given the complexity of the pipeline (multiple pretrained models, reward oracles, structure predictors) across three very different domains.
